To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Na-Ca exchange current is a function of both the membrane potential and the cytoplasmic Ca2+ concentration, and that the Na-Cal exchange current can be separated from the other membrane currents by blocking the Ca2+ channels, the Na+ channels, and the Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmatic reticulum with drugs.
the Na-Ca exchanger in guinea pig ventricular cells is electrogenic and has a stoichiometry of 3:1.

(a) in guinea-pig cardiac cells, Na-Ca exchange current is a major component of membrane current, (b) INaCa can be measured by voltage clamp, (c) INaCa is a function of [Ca]i, and (d) INaCa depends on the membrane voltage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the sodium-calcium exchange mechanism in cardiac myocytes.
the mechanism of the electrogenic sodium‐calcium exchange current in cardiac muscle cells.
the role of calcium and calcium binding proteins in the control of gene expression in the heart.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na‐Ca exchange is electrogenic and that the electrochemical gradient for Na is the driving force for the exchange of Ca for Na.
the data are consistent with the existence of a simultaneous step exchange mechanism, in which the internal site for Ca2+, but not the external, is assumed to be saturated.
the results support a model based on a sequential mechanism in which the internal Ca2+ binding site is only partially filled.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found a very strong dependence of INaCa on membrane potential, and that we found that INaCa was a very good predictor of the Ca transient.
the exchange current is not constant, but depends on the driving force and the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.

we have shown that Na‐Ca exchange in guinea pig ventricular myocytes operates in the direction of Na efflux and Ca influx at all potentials, and that the exchange current is not saturated by the Ca concentration at physiological values of this variable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Na/Ca exchanger can contribute to the development of arrhythmias.
the Na-Ca exchanger can operate in the reverse mode, i.e., to extrude Na+ in exchange for Ca2+ uptake, and that it is electrogenic, i.e., the exchanger current (INa-Ca) is not zero.
the sodium-calcium exchange current can be recorded in single cardiac cells, and that the current is carried by sodium ions.
